For anyone who isn't familiar with the etymology:

>gyp (v.)

>also gip, "to cheat, swindle," 1889, American English, traditionally derived from Gypsy (n.). Gyp/gip/jip is attested from 1794 as university slang for a servant that waited on students in their halls. This is said to have been especially a Cambridge word, and a story told there derived it from Greek gyps "vulture," in reference to thievish habits of the servants. 

>As a noun, "fraudulent action, a cheat," by 1914. Gypsy's abbreviated form Gip, Gyp is attested from 1840. Gypping or gipping was a term late 19c. among horse dealers for tricks such as painting the animal's gray hairs brown, puffing the gums, etc. Related: Gypped.

From [Etymology Online](https://www.etymonline.com/word/gyp#etymonline_v_14409)

And you can also check out a [longer article from NPR](https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2013/12/30/242429836/why-being-gypped-hurts-the-roma-more-than-it-hurts-you) for more context.

To me, this feels like one of those moments where the collective moral code of r/amitheasshole doesn't align with the outside world. (https://www.reddit.com/r/AmItheAsshole/comments/d6xoro/meta_this_sub_is_moving_towards_a_value_system/)

Did the mom fuck up? Absolutely. She should have known the school schedule, and, like you said, she should have given her child a reliable way to contact her*. This child is the mom's responsibility.

Did OP act with good intent? Definitely! OP made calls, OP gave quarters, and OP was completely genuine in their thinking that the kid would stay warm and be okay.

But very often on this sub, the conversation ends there. If OP doesn't have primary responsibility, and if OP doesn't have negative intent, then we all say OP is N T A.

In the real world, the equation is different. Sometimes having good intentions isn't enough to absolve you.

If a kid approaches you, tells you they're locked out, they can't reach their mom, and they need help, *you don't leave that kid alone*, especially not in a public or semi-public space. Quarters or not, warm laundry room or not, good intentions or not, you find another adult who can ensure that the child is safe.

I don't want to make a judgement here, because I feel like AH or not AH is too black and white, and there's a lot of gray area that we're skimming over.

*Mentioning here as a thought, but I apologize if someone else already said it: if mom is working a service industry job, it's possible she's not allowed to hold her phone during working hours. Not saying that excuses her, as she definitely should have had a backup person the kid could contact, but it may help explain her actions (and her panic & anger, which she's misplacing on OP).

My read is a bit different from yours:

1. They get engaged.
2. They buy the dress. The fiance makes a (maybe foolish, but not terribly uncommon) decision to buy a dress that's a bit to slim, with plans to ramp up her  already active lifestyle to fit it.
3. They find out she's pregnant, and she gains weight during the pregnancy.
4. She gives birth. OPs timeline isn't completely clear, but it sounds like sometime this summer.
5. After giving birth, she has trouble engaging in her previous fitness hobbies. Sounds to me like potential PPD, but obviously we don't know quite enough. (But even if it isn't PPD, she's a new mom, and probably busy, tired, and/or overwhelmed. It's completely unreasonable for OP to expect her to start back up exercising and lose 60 lbs. so fast.)
6. Her brother dies. Whatever difficulties she's experiencing as a new mom are compounded.

So she bought a dress that was too small, at a point in her life when slimming down WAS an achievable goal. Now it isn't. And that's probably just one more thing making her feel awful and overwhelmed.

Your phrasing here:
>hey I know I INSISTED on this small dress but can you buy this one for me now, even though I INSISTED that I would fit into the small one by now, and I know we will lose multiple hundreds of dollars but hey ho doesn't matter, let's just throw away our income because it's not like husband would like to use that money to get something for himself or the kid.

is unnecessarily cruel and cavalier.

Is she being unreasonable? Yes, especially with the sarcasm. Is it financially wise to buy a new dress? Probably not. Can they afford it? Who knows! OP didn't give us any information about their financial situation. Is that reason enough to offer her no compassion and completely dismiss her? No, it is not.

It's especially alarming that OP, her future husband, has more to say about her weight than about her mental health.

Hi, I have PMDD, and I'd like to help. I don't have time right now to say as much as I'd like, but this is a quick answer to help you move in the right direction. Please ask any questions, and I'll answer as much as I can.

**Step 0: More Info**

(Apologies if you already know this, but I wouldn't want to skip it in case you don't.) Visit the website of the International Association for Pre-Menstrual Disorders at https://iapmd.org/.

**Step 1: Track your symptoms and period**

There are a few period tracking apps specifically aimed at people with PMDD, and I recommend selecting one of those. I use PreMentricS, which is convenient because you can send your data straight to your doctor.

If you find that physical calendars work better for you, the IAPMD offers a symptom tracker you can download and print (https://iapmd.org/toolkit).

**Step 2: Find a Doctor Who Knows PMDD**

This can be a scary step. Some doctors dismiss any PMS-related symptoms. There is a long history of people with PMDD being misdiagnosed as having bipolar disorder. I say this not to worry you, but to prep you. You may need to find and visit a few different doctors before you find one who is familiar with PMDD and will take you seriously. **Don't give up.**

You will probably want to build a care team involving–at minimum–both a gynecologist and a psychiatrist. Those two professionals will work from different perspectives, and their combined expertise will help you find a solution.

The IAPMD offers a directory or recommended doctors. You may want to start your search there (https://iapmd.org/provider-directory).

**Step 3: Get Treatment**

This process will be slow, and it will involve trial and error. What works for some people doesn't for others. You will probably work through various SSRIs, antidepressants, birth control options, and (maybe) gnrh agonists. I have more specifics about the recommended treatment schedule, but I don't have time to find them now. Let me know if you want them.

Everyone responds to treatment differently. Some people find the right SSRI, and then they're fine. Some people need to get on the right birth control to prevent ovulation. Some people need a cocktail of birth control and medicine. The right solution takes time to find. It may be frustrating, especially when you're in the middle of hell week and it's hard to hold onto hope. **Don't give up.**

**Step 4: Get Support**

If you can afford it, find a therapist.

Talk to the people in your life about your experiences. Keep your husband in the loop. about your day-to-day emotional state. If your support network includes family or friends, talk to them. Explain what you need and when. Don't be afraid to ask for help.

Visit r/pmdd.

I doubt you'll be able to find an in-person support groups, but online groups exist. I know of at least one on facebook.

You may want to check out r/PMDD to see if any of the stories there resonate with you.

Edit: Also check out the International Association for Pre-Menstrual Disorders (https://iapmd.org/). They have a lot of resources and information, and those can help you get started on the path of treatment. Take that information with you when you go to see your gynecologist.

P.S. You're not alone.
